name: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty

lead: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty rebuilds or reshapes the nose using cartilage taken from your own rib. People turn to it for major bridge reconstruction, revision surgery and extended grafts that give the nose firm support and a new shape.

Carved rib cartilage supplies large, sturdy grafts for the nasal bridge and tip support, which septal or ear cartilage often cannot provide. A retrospective cohort of 58 rib graft patients treated from 2000 to 2009 assessed graft stability, warping, revision and donor-site problems; the published evidence is made up of small surgeon case series.

paras: It is done by a surgeon under anesthesia as part of a larger rhinoplasty, usually when septal cartilage is insufficient or a previous operation has used it up. The surgeon harvests rib cartilage through a chest incision, carves it into grafts such as a columellar strut or bridge graft, and builds them into the nose. The nose changes shape right away under swelling, and the final look settles as the swelling goes down over the following months.

The procedure adds a second surgical site on the chest, and studies track donor-site problems and graft warping. Rhinoplasty revision rates are roughly 5 to 20 percent overall. It is surgery with the general risks of anesthesia and rhinoplasty.

angle.text: Harvested rib cartilage is carved into large structural grafts that rebuild the bridge and tip, so the nose is visibly reshaped. Surgeons use it when septal cartilage is not enough, mainly for major reconstruction and revision rhinoplasty. Published results come from small surgeon series.

lead: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty, also called costal cartilage rhinoplasty, is nose surgery in which cartilage harvested from the patient's own rib is carved into structural grafts. People pursue it to get a nose with more projection, a straighter or higher bridge, a longer or better-supported tip, or a rebuilt framework after earlier surgery, changes that need more graft material than the nose itself can supply. General references note that septal cartilage is the preferred graft source and that rib or ear cartilage is used when septal cartilage is insufficient, as is common in revision cases.[1]

It is most associated with major dorsal reconstruction, revision cases, Asian rhinoplasty and extended grafts such as the columellar strut and septal extension graft. A review in Facial Plastic Surgery describes costal cartilage as abundant, biocompatible and versatile, with a steady increase in its use in Asian rhinoplasty.[2] Because the graft is the patient's own tissue, it avoids the rejection and implant-related complications that surgeons associate with synthetic materials such as silicone.[1][3]

Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and cohorts. A retrospective cohort of 58 rib graft patients treated from 2000 to 2009 assessed graft stability, warping, need for revision and donor-site morbidity, and a 2025 meta-analysis of six studies with 888 patients pooled a complication rate of roughly 7 to 8 percent, mostly minor.[4][5] The operation adds a second surgical site on the chest, which the literature treats as part of the procedure's trade-offs.[2]

paras: Rhinoplasty references list septal cartilage as the first choice for grafts, with rib or ear cartilage used when septal cartilage is not enough, and bone or synthetic implants as further options [1]. Rib cartilage provides a larger quantity of material, which is why it is described for extensive reconstructions [4]. Wikipedia notes that donor rib cartilage is sometimes used when the patient's own cartilage is unsuitable, and that a septal extension graft gives greater control over tip support than a columellar strut [1].

The costal cartilages are the flexible bars that join the ribs to the breastbone. They provide a much larger volume of firm, straight-grained cartilage than the nasal septum or the ear, so a single harvest can supply dorsal onlay grafts, spreader grafts, tip grafts and struts. Some authors graft cartilage together with a segment of rib bone, the osseocartilaginous technique, for dorsal augmentation.[4] Others use diced cartilage to soften the edges of a graft so they are not visible under the skin.[6] Wikipedia notes that for a collapsed bridge, rib, ear or cranial bone grafts can restore nasal contour, and that for reconstruction surgeons prefer autologous cartilage and bone grafts over artificial prostheses because of lower rates of rejection and complications.[1]

In Asian rhinoplasty, anatomy such as a low dorsum, short columella and thick-skinned tip has often been addressed with silicone implants, but surgeons report that silicone-related complications and rising revision rates have pushed some towards autologous rib cartilage [3]. A 2020 paper describes combining diced costal cartilage with spreader grafts to hide graft margins and smooth the dorsum, in 6 patients followed for a mean of 15 months, 5 of whom were very satisfied [6]. A 2024 paper from Zhejiang describes building the framework from the sixth costal cartilage, as strut, integrated tip graft and septal extension graft, in 65 patients aged 19-43, and reported statistically significant improvement in measured aesthetic indices at 9 months with no short-term complications [7].

Descriptions of the operation in the literature share a general sequence: the surgeon harvests a piece of costal cartilage through a small chest incision, shapes it into the grafts the nose needs, and places them through an open or closed nasal approach. A 2015 technique paper describes anchoring an extended columellar strut with rib graft to support and lengthen the tip.[8] The 2024 Zhejiang series built a framework from the sixth costal cartilage, using a columellar strut, an integrated tip graft and septal extension grafts sutured together.[7]

Septal extension grafts and columellar struts both support the tip; Wikipedia says septal extension grafts give greater control and show fewer changes over time.[1] Because cartilage can warp as it heals, reviews discuss carving and fixation techniques intended to reduce that tendency.[2] Calcification of the rib cartilage has also been studied: a Chinese comparison of 35 patients with extensive calcification against 35 without reported comparable measurements and satisfaction.[9]

Reconstruction of the nose is one of the oldest surgical subjects, with descriptions in ancient Egyptian and Indian texts and a skin-flap method described by Tagliacozzi in 1597.[1] Cartilage grafts entered modern practice with the development of closed and open rhinoplasty in the late 19th and 20th centuries; Wikipedia credits John Orlando Roe with the first modern closed rhinoplasty in 1887 and Rethi with introducing the open approach in 1934.[1] Revision rhinoplasty, which the article puts at 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties, is where surgeons usually rebuild support with ear or rib cartilage.[1]

Silicone implants were long used in Asian countries to augment and lengthen the nose; surgeons writing in Seminars in Plastic Surgery in 2015 reported silicone-related complications and rising revision surgery, and described rib cartilage as an alternative that gives strong support and enough material to correct deformed structure.[3] Use in this setting has increased steadily, according to the 2020 review.[2]

In the 58-patient retrospective study, investigators evaluated graft viability, mobility, warping, maintenance of dorsal projection, airway function, revision rates and donor-site problems through telephone follow-up; the authors described the technique as stable and predictable for major dorsal reconstruction [4]. A comparison of 35 patients with extensively calcified costal cartilage against 35 without found no significant difference in nose measurements or satisfaction (ROE scores improved significantly in both groups), with one infection in each group [9].

Surgeons writing in Seminars in Plastic Surgery state that, performed properly by an experienced operator, rib rhinoplasty gives long-lasting results with low risk.[3] The 2025 meta-analysis, which pooled six studies with at least six months of follow-up, described rib cartilage as a preferred approach for complex nasal reconstruction and reported pooled complication rates of 7 percent (fixed-effects) and 8 percent (random-effects) with substantial heterogeneity between studies.[5] In the 6-patient diced-cartilage series, none needed removal or revision of the graft at a mean follow-up of 15 months.[6]

Using rib adds a second surgical site. The 2011 study specifically assessed donor-site morbidity and graft warping as outcomes [4]. The Facial Plastic Surgery review lists warping, infection and displacement among graft complications and pneumothorax, pain and chest scars among donor-site problems, and states many can be minimised by recommended techniques [2]. The 2025 meta-analysis found complications predominantly minor, including infection, warping and graft problems, with substantial heterogeneity between studies [5]. General rhinoplasty references report that revision surgery accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations [1].

Donor-site problems named in the literature are pneumothorax, pain and chest scarring.[2] In the 2022 Chinese series, one patient in each group developed an infection after surgery.[9] Graft warping can alter the nasal line over time, and displacement of a graft is a reported complication.[2] The authors of the 2025 meta-analysis characterised most complications as minor.[5]

Published human data consist of a retrospective cohort of 58 patients [4], a technique paper on anchoring an extended columellar strut [8], the 2025 meta-analysis of 888 patients [5], comparison and technique series from China [6][7][9], and reviews of complications [2]. A registered study of allograft cartilage in cosmetic and reconstructive rhinoplasty (NCT05566808, 50 participants, completed) is listed, though it concerns a different graft source [10]. No randomized trials of rib cartilage were found.
